label: CAMPAIGN 11
title: The Language of Arrival
firewall: We track how the words have been used and how fast they are winning, not whether the underlying politics is correct.
summary: The naming war has a new leader and it is nobody's slogan. Across a 180-day full-text window, 'noncitizen' is up 89.9% while 'undocumented' is down 23.4% and 'illegal alien' is flat at -1.8%. The two words that have carried the argument for two decades — one the advocacy term, one the statutory term — are both losing ground to an administrative negative that takes no side at all. A category stated as an absence of citizenship is displacing both the word that names a missing document and the word that names an unlawful entry.
anchor: Through 2026 the argument over arrival stayed loud, and the words used to hold it quietly changed hands. Across seventeen measured terms the vocabulary of position cooled while the vocabulary of status and process climbed. The fight did not move to the border; it moved to the file.
thesis: The naming war has a new leader and it is nobody's slogan. Across a 180-day full-text window, 'noncitizen' is up 89.9% while 'undocumented' is down 23.4% and 'illegal alien' is flat at -1.8%. The two words that have carried the argument for two decades — one the advocacy term, one the statutory term — are both losing ground to an administrative negative that takes no side at all. A category stated as an absence of citizenship is displacing both the word that names a missing document and the word that names an unlawful entry.

The same movement runs through the machinery. 'Work permit' is up 79.8% and 'removal proceedings' up 66.8%, while 'border security' is down 8.1% and 'detention' down 23.5%. The political framings cool with them: 'sanctuary city' -30.0%, 'open borders' -17.5%. What is rising is the language of status, permission and docket; what is falling is the language of crossing, position and refuge. That is the cycle's measured finding, and it was not the one this campaign expected to make.

definingTension.note: The cycle's measured collision and the campaign's spine. Both name the same person; one describes a missing document, the other an absent citizenship. Measured over 90 days, 'noncitizen' is up 89.9% and 'undocumented' is down 23.4%. The advocacy term that won the style guides is losing ground to an administrative description that concedes nothing and claims nothing.

clusters.name: What people are called
clusters.blurb: The six nouns the argument reaches for when it has to name a person: the advocacy term, the statutory term, the treaty term, the claim term, the umbrella term, and the administrative term. Each chooses what to foreground — a missing document, an unlawful entry, a recognised status, a filed claim, a movement, or an absence of citizenship — and the choice is made before any argument begins.

clusters.name: The machinery
clusters.blurb: The vocabulary of the system itself: the expulsion and the docket that produces it, the custody between arrival and outcome, the lawful door, the permission to work, and the frame that treats the border as a security object. These are the words that appear on notices and in appropriations, and they describe process rather than position.

clusters.name: The contested framings
clusters.blurb: The phrases that turn arrival into a verdict: scale attached to a process, departure recast as a decision, a cooperation policy named as refuge, a position attributed to opponents, and reform described as a route. Each is used by more than one side, and each is doing argumentative work before it describes anything.

pillars.title: The word that's winning: 'noncitizen,' not either of the ones we argue about
pillars.body: The cycle's lede, and it is measured. Two decades of dispute between 'undocumented' and 'illegal alien' has produced a third winner that belongs to neither camp. 'Noncitizen' is up 89.9% over 90 days; the two contenders are down 23.4% and 1.8%. A word chosen for administrative neutrality is absorbing the coverage that two words chosen for their charge are losing.

pillars.title: The argument moved from the border to the paperwork
pillars.body: Read across the clusters, the pattern is consistent: status and process vocabulary rises — 'work permit' +79.8%, 'removal proceedings' +66.8%, 'port of entry' +6.5% — while position vocabulary falls — 'border security' -8.1%, 'sanctuary city' -30.0%, 'open borders' -17.5%. The coverage is relocating from where people arrive to what happens to their file afterwards.

pillars.title: 'Migrant' is the umbrella that held
pillars.body: At a corpus density of 0.3045 it is the densest term in the set — denser than 'deportation' — and it is up 38.2% over 90 days. The one noun that specifies neither cause nor claim is both the most used and still rising, which is what a word looks like when every side can say it without conceding anything.

tensions.title: 'noncitizen' vs 'undocumented'
tensions.body: The cycle's measured collision and the campaign's spine. Both name the same person; one describes a missing document, the other an absent citizenship. Measured over 90 days, 'noncitizen' is up 89.9% and 'undocumented' is down 23.4%. The advocacy term that won the style guides is losing ground to an administrative description that concedes nothing and claims nothing.

tensions.title: 'illegal alien' holds while 'undocumented' falls
tensions.body: The expected story was a contest between these two. Measurement declines it: 'illegal alien' is effectively flat at -1.8% while 'undocumented' falls 23.4%. Neither is winning the naming war. The statutory term is not surging; the advocacy term is simply receding faster, and a third word is taking the ground both vacated.

tensions.title: 'work permit' vs 'border security'
tensions.body: Permission to work is up 79.8%; the border framed as a security object is down 8.1%. The economic question — who may work, and after how long — is gaining the coverage that the enforcement frame is losing. The argument is migrating from the line on the map to the document in the file.

tensions.title: 'removal proceedings' vs 'detention'
tensions.body: Inside the machinery the docket rises and the custody falls: 'removal proceedings' up 66.8%, 'detention' down 23.5%. The process word is displacing the condition word, which moves the account of what happens to people from a place to a procedure.

tensions.title: Three political framings cool, two rise
tensions.body: 'Sanctuary city' is down 30.0%, 'open borders' down 17.5%, 'self-deportation' down 3.5%. Two of the phrases built to carry a verdict gained against that drift: 'legal pathway' at +18.2% and 'mass deportation' at +10.9%. The language that argues is thinning while the language that processes thickens.

terms.whereContested: Contested over whether the claim is the defining fact or whether the manner of entry is, and over backlog as a description of the system.
